Importers are advised to adopt comprehensive compliance measures and coordinate closely with regulatory authorities.

‍

Import Permits Philippines

‍

Compliance Risks Article

‍

Regulatory Oversight and Environmental Compliance

‍

The importation of chemicals is tightly regulated due to potential risks to public health, workplace safety, and the environment. Importers must secure import permits from relevant agencies such as the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), depending on the type of chemical. These permits ensure that substances entering the country meet environmental standards and do not pose undue hazards.

‍

Beyond permits, importers must comply with environmental regulations such as the Philippine Clean Air Act and the Toxic Substances and Hazardous and Nuclear Wastes Control Act (RA 6969). These laws mandate proper documentation of chemical composition, toxicity levels, and safe disposal methods. Failure to comply can lead to fines, suspension of import rights, or even criminal liability.

‍

Customs Clearance Process

‍

Hazardous Substances and Special Clearances

‍

Certain chemicals particularly those classified as hazardous substances require additional clearance before importation. These include industrial solvents, pesticides, and raw materials used in manufacturing that may pose risks if mishandled. Importers must submit Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) and secure clearance from agencies like the Environmental Management Bureau (EMB).

‍

Storage and handling requirements are equally critical. Warehouses must be certified for chemical storage, with fire suppression systems and spill containment measures in place. Transportation must follow strict guidelines, including labeling, packaging, and route planning to minimize risks during transit.

‍

Customs Classification and Declaration

‍

From a customs perspective, accurate classification under the Harmonized System (HS) Code is essential. Misclassification - whether intentional or accidental - can lead to penalties, shipment delays, or outright seizure of goods. Importers must declare the exact chemical composition, intended use, and value of the goods.

‍

Customs clearance also requires coordination with the Bureau of Customs (BOC), which may conduct inspections to verify compliance. Importers should prepare for possible laboratory testing of samples to confirm the declared properties of the chemicals.

Name: ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (AJCEPA)
Summary: Learn about the ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (AJCEPA), its objectives, principles, tariff commitments, and benefits for Philippine trade and investment.
Post body:
The ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (AJCEPA) is a free trade agreement between the ten ASEAN Member States and Japan. It was established to strengthen economic relations, expand market access, improve trade facilitation, and promote investment cooperation between ASEAN countries and Japan.

‍

The agreement covers Trade in Goods (TIG), Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS), Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT), Trade in Services, Trade in Investment, and Economic Cooperation and Trade Facilitation. AJCEPA aims to gradually establish a stronger free trade area over a ten-year period while supporting ASEAN economic integration. Philippine importers dealing with Japanese goods should also review the bilateral Philippines-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (PJEPA), which may offer additional benefits.

‍

Basic Principles of AJCEPA

  • Participation of all ASEAN Member States and Japan
  • Promotion of liberalization, trade facilitation, and cooperation
  • Reciprocity, transparency, and mutual benefit
  • Consistency with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules
  • Recognition of different development levels among ASEAN members
  • Flexibility for sensitive sectors in ASEAN countries and Japan
  • Support through technical cooperation and capacity building

‍

Objectives of AJCEPA

  • Strengthen economic integration between ASEAN and Japan
  • Improve the global competitiveness of ASEAN and Japan
  • Liberalize trade in goods and services progressively
  • Create a transparent and liberal investment environment
  • Promote new areas of economic cooperation
  • Reduce development gaps among ASEAN Member States

‍

Trade Facilitation and Cooperation Areas

AJCEPA also includes cooperation in strategic sectors:

  • Customs and Trade Procedures - Simplification, harmonization, and computerization of customs procedures to speed up trade flows. This reduces the risk of demurrage and detention charges caused by processing delays.
  • Business Environment - Improving the regulatory and investment climate to attract investors.
  • Intellectual Property Rights - Support for ASEAN countries in improving IP systems and joining international IP agreements.
  • Energy Cooperation - Collaboration in oil stockpiling, natural gas use, and energy efficiency.
  • Information and Communications Technology (ICT) - Development of ICT infrastructure, legal systems, and IT human resources.

‍

Philippine AJCEPA Tariff Highlights

Based on the tariff schedule, a large majority of Philippine tariff lines under AJCEPA are at 0% tariff rates from 2018 onwards, covering around 88.5% of tariff lines. This reflects the Philippines' commitment to reducing trade barriers and increasing access to Japanese and ASEAN markets. For a full breakdown of import cost computation, see our Importation Costs Breakdown.

‍

Why AJCEPA Matters to Philippine Businesses

AJCEPA provides Philippine exporters, importers, and investors with significant opportunities through lower tariffs, easier customs procedures, and stronger economic cooperation with Japan and ASEAN partners. It helps businesses become more competitive while encouraging foreign direct investment and technology transfer. For Philippine companies involved in manufacturing, agriculture, electronics, automotive parts, and services, AJCEPA remains an important framework for regional trade growth.

Name: Importation Timelines and Delays Philippines
Summary: Typical importation timelines in the Philippines, common causes of delays, and how to keep your shipments on schedule.
Post body:
Knowing the typical timelines involved in Philippine importation helps businesses plan their supply chains and reduce the risk of unexpected delays. While timelines vary depending on the goods, the port of entry, and the completeness of documentation, the general stages follow a predictable sequence.

‍

Typical Importation Timeline

‍

Pre-Arrival (2-4 weeks before shipment)

  • Secure BOC accreditation (if not yet registered)
  • Obtain regulatory permits from relevant agencies (FDA, DA, DTI, etc.)
  • Prepare and finalize all shipping documents

‍

Shipment in Transit (days to weeks depending on origin)

  • Sea freight from Asia: approximately 5-14 days
  • Sea freight from the US/Europe: approximately 20-35 days
  • Air freight: approximately 1-5 days

‍

Arrival and Port Processing (1-5 working days, standard)

  • Goods declaration filed upon or before arrival
  • Lane assignment by the customs selectivity system
  • Green Lane: release within 1-2 working days
  • Yellow Lane: documentary review adds 1-3 working days
  • Red Lane: physical inspection adds 3-7 working days or more

‍

Payment and Release (1-2 working days after assessment)

  • Duties and taxes assessed and payment processed
  • ATRIG issued for regulated goods
  • Delivery order secured from shipping line
  • Port charges settled and gate pass issued

‍

Common Causes of Delays

  • Incomplete or inaccurate goods declaration
  • Missing or late permits from regulatory agencies
  • Discrepancies between documents (value, quantity, description)
  • Physical inspection (Red Lane assignment)
  • Late BOC accreditation or NRI application
  • Port congestion or vessel delays
  • Outstanding storage or arrastre charges

‍

How to Minimize Delays

  • Secure permits and accreditation well before the shipment departs
  • Submit complete and accurate documentation
  • Work with a licensed customs broker who knows the system
  • Monitor your shipment status and respond quickly to any requests from customs

‍

Most delays in Philippine customs are avoidable with proper planning. The earlier you prepare your documents and permits, the smoother your clearance will be.

Name: Import Documentation Checklist
Summary: Complete checklist of documents required for importing goods into the Philippines - commercial invoice, packing list, permits, and more.
Post body:
Importation into the Philippines requires submitting various documents to the Bureau of Customs and other regulatory agencies. Incomplete or inconsistent documentation is one of the most common reasons shipments get delayed at customs.

‍

Core Documents

‍

Commercial Invoice

Shows seller and buyer details, description of goods, unit price and total value. This is the main basis for customs valuation.

‍

Packing List

Provides a breakdown of packages, quantity per item, and weight and dimensions. This helps customs verify the physical shipment.

‍

Bill of Lading / Airway Bill

Serves as proof of shipment, a transport document, and reference for cargo release.

‍

Supporting Documents

Depending on the shipment, you may also need:

  • Import Permits - required for regulated goods - see our Import Permits and Government Agencies guide - issued by agencies such as the FDA, Department of Agriculture, and Department of Trade and Industry, among others.
  • Certificate of Origin - used to determine tariff rates and apply preferential trade agreements.
  • Insurance Documents - used for valuation purposes and in computing duties and taxes.

‍

Practical Tips

  • Make sure product descriptions are clear, specific, and detailed.
  • Values must be consistent across all documents.
  • Avoid generic terms like "parts" or "equipment".
  • Double-check quantities and weights.

‍

Good documentation doesn't just help with compliance - it speeds up clearance and reduces the risk of issues. One missing document can lead to penalties or delays. A licensed customs broker can help make sure everything is in order before your shipment arrives.

Name: Pharmaceutical and Medical Device Importation in the Philippines
Summary: Learn how to import pharmaceuticals and medical devices into the Philippines, including FDA permits, compliance, and customs process.
Post body:
The importation of pharmaceuticals and medical devices into the Philippines is strictly regulated due to their direct impact on public health and safety. Government agencies, particularly the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), enforce rigorous standards to ensure that all imported products are safe, effective, and of high quality. Businesses involved in this sector must understand that compliance is not optional but a critical requirement before products can enter the Philippine market.

‍

To operate legally, importers must first secure a License to Operate (LTO) from the FDA. In addition, each pharmaceutical product or medical device must undergo a registration process before it can be imported and distributed. Depending on the type and classification of the product, additional approvals may be required, making import permits in the Philippines an essential part of the process. These permits ensure that regulated goods meet safety and quality standards prior to shipment and entry into the country.

‍

Accurate tariff classification is also crucial in pharmaceutical importation, as it determines the applicable duties, taxes, and regulatory controls for each product. Misclassification can lead to compliance issues, shipment delays, or financial penalties. Given the technical nature of pharmaceutical and medical device products, classification often requires detailed product knowledge and careful review of customs regulations.

‍

From a customs perspective, importers must follow the standard customs clearance process, which includes lodging the goods declaration, submitting complete documentation, and paying the appropriate duties and taxes. However, compared to other industries, pharmaceutical shipments are typically subject to stricter inspections and verification procedures. Authorities may closely examine supporting documents, including product registrations, certificates, and permits, before allowing release of goods.

‍

Common challenges in this sector include delays in FDA product registration, incomplete or inconsistent documentation, and non-compliance with labeling and packaging standards. These issues can result in shipment holds, additional costs, or rejection of goods. Due to the complexity of both regulatory and customs requirements, businesses are strongly encouraged to seek professional guidance to ensure full compliance and a more efficient importation process.

Name: Personal and Household Effects of Travelers, Tourists, and Foreign Consultants
Summary: Learn how personal effects and foreign consultants' goods are conditionally exempt from duties and taxes including requirements and process with the Bureau of Customs.
Post body:
Under CAO 06-2020, the Philippines allows conditional tax and duty exemption for goods brought in for personal use, temporary stay, or professional needs. This covers travelers' and tourists' personal effects such as clothing, toiletries, personal accessories, portable tools, instruments, theatrical costumes, and other items needed during the trip. It also includes personal and household effects and vehicles owned by foreign consultants and experts working in the country.

‍

Personal Effects of Travelers and Tourists

‍

Who May Avail

  • Foreign tourists entering the Philippines
  • Returning travelers bringing personal belongings
  • Individuals temporarily visiting the country

The exemption applies only if goods are not intended for sale, barter, hire, or transfer to other persons.

‍

Documentary Requirements

  • Goods Declaration
  • Import Bill of Lading or Air Waybill
  • Import Invoice and Packing List
  • Written commitment OR Security (100% of duties and taxes)

‍

Security Requirement

A security equivalent to 100% of duties, taxes, and charges is required, conditioned on exportation of goods within 3 months or payment of duties and taxes if not re-exported. An extension of up to 3 additional months may be granted by Customs.

‍

Process for Conditional Exemption

  1. Arrival of Goods - Travelers or importers bring or ship personal effects into the Philippines.
  2. Filing of Goods Declaration - Submit declaration and supporting import documents to Customs.
  3. Submission of Requirements - Present bill of lading/air waybill, invoice, packing list, and security or written undertaking.
  4. Evaluation by Customs - The BOC assesses whether items qualify as personal effects under CAO 06-2020.
  5. Approval of Conditional Exemption - If compliant, goods are released conditionally without immediate payment of duties and taxes.
  6. Monitoring Period - Goods must be exported or duties paid within 3 months (extendable once).

‍

Personal Effects and Vehicles of Foreign Consultants and Experts

‍

Who May Avail

  • Foreign consultants hired by the Philippine government
  • Foreign experts rendering official services in the Philippines
  • Accompanying family members and staff

Items must match the consultant's role or assignment and serve only personal or professional use - not for commercial purposes.

‍

Documentary Requirements

  • Tax Exemption Indorsement (TEI) with supporting documents
  • Goods Declaration
  • Import Bill of Lading or Air Waybill
  • Import Invoice and Packing List
  • Security OR written commitment (100% of duties and taxes)

‍

Process for Conditional Exemption

  1. Arrival of Goods - Household effects or vehicles are imported into the Philippines.
  2. Filing of TEI and Import Documents - Importer submits Tax Exemption Indorsement and supporting documents.
  3. Submission of Security or Commitment - Provide bond or written undertaking for re-export or payment of duties.
  4. Customs Evaluation and Approval - Customs verifies eligibility based on contract and necessity of goods.
  5. Conditional Release - Goods are released without immediate payment of duties and taxes.
  6. End-of-Term Compliance - Upon expiration of contract, goods must be re-exported or duties and taxes must be paid within the allowed period (up to 3 months extension possible).

‍

Basis: CAO 06-2020

Name: Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP)
Summary: Explore the RCEP framework, including tariff commitments, rules of origin, and trade in goods and services across the Asia-Pacific region.
Post body:
The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is established as a free trade area among the Member States of ASEAN and its partners, including Australia, China, Japan, Korea, and New Zealand. The agreement is designed to broaden and deepen regional economic integration, strengthen growth, and advance cooperation through a modern and comprehensive framework. As the world's largest free trade agreement by geographic coverage, RCEP has significant implications for import duties and taxes in the Philippines.

‍

Primary Objectives

  • Parties establish a mutually beneficial partnership to facilitate regional trade and investment.
  • The agreement progressively liberalizes trade in goods through the elimination of tariff and non-tariff barriers.
  • RCEP expands trade in services with substantial sectoral coverage to eliminate discriminatory measures.
  • The framework creates a competitive investment environment to enhance opportunities and protection for investors.

‍

Tariff Commitments

  • Parties reduce or eliminate customs duties on originating goods as specified in each Party's Schedule of Tariff Commitments.
  • Exporters utilize the most-favored-nation (MFN) applied rate if it is lower than the rate provided in the RCEP Schedule.
  • Two or more Parties may accelerate or improve tariff commitments unilaterally or through mutual consent.

‍

Non-Tariff Measures

The agreement addresses obstacles to trade to prevent unnecessary barriers:

  • Quantitative Restrictions - Parties generally eliminate prohibitions or restrictions on imports and exports, except in accordance with WTO rights.
  • Import Licensing - Parties implement procedures in a transparent manner and notify other Parties to ensure predictability.
  • Technical Consultations - A Party may request consultations if it considers that a measure adversely affects trade, with a goal of reaching a solution within 180 days.

‍

Temporary Admission and Transit

  • Customs territories conditionally relieve goods from import duties if the owner brings them in for specific purposes (e.g., display or repair) and intends to re-export them.
  • The agreement grants duty-free temporary admission for containers and pallets used in international traffic, regardless of their origin.
  • Parties grant duty-free entry to samples of no commercial value from other Parties.

‍

Rules of Origin (ROO)

Authorities must determine originating status for a good to qualify for preferential tariff treatment. A good qualifies as originating if it meets one of the following:

  • Wholly Obtained or Produced - A Party obtains the good entirely within its territory.
  • Produced Exclusively from Originating Materials - A producer creates the good using materials that already qualify as originating from one or more Parties.
  • Product-Specific Rules (PSR) - The product satisfies specific requirements such as a Change in Tariff Classification (CTC) or a Regional Value Content (RVC) threshold.

For a broader explanation of how rules of origin work, see our Rules of Origin Guide.

‍

Operational Certification

  • Proof of Origin - Importers claim preferential treatment via a Certificate of Origin issued by an authorized body, or a Declaration of Origin by an approved exporter.
  • Back-to-Back Proof of Origin - An intermediate Party may issue this for goods that do not undergo further processing beyond logistics or preservation.
  • Record-Keeping - Exporters, producers, and importers must retain all records necessary to prove originating status for at least three years. This aligns with the record-keeping requirements under Post-Clearance Audit procedures.

Name: Lifting of Abandonment Process in Philippine Customs
Summary: How to apply for lifting of abandonment for imported goods held by the Bureau of Customs in the Philippines.
Post body:
Under Philippine customs law, imported goods that are not claimed or processed within a prescribed period are subject to abandonment. Once declared abandoned, the Bureau of Customs may dispose of the goods - typically through auction or destruction. Importers may apply to lift the abandonment and recover their shipment, subject to specific requirements.

‍

What Is Abandonment?

Abandonment occurs when an importer fails to file the goods declaration or claim the shipment within the allowable period under the Customs Modernization and Tariff Act. There are two types:

  • Express Abandonment - The importer formally renounces ownership of the goods in writing.
  • Implied Abandonment - The importer fails to act within the prescribed period, triggering automatic abandonment.

‍

Prescribed Periods

  • Goods must generally be claimed and a goods declaration filed within 30 days from the date of discharge for sea cargo
  • For air cargo, the period is typically shorter
  • Failure to act within these periods results in implied abandonment

‍

Lifting of Abandonment

An importer may apply to lift the abandonment before the goods are disposed of by customs. The process generally involves:

  1. Filing a formal application for lifting of abandonment with the Bureau of Customs
  2. Submitting required documents including the bill of lading, commercial invoice, and proof of ownership
  3. Payment of storage, arrastre, and other accrued charges
  4. Payment of applicable duties and taxes
  5. Compliance with any permit or regulatory requirements for the goods
  6. Approval by the Collector of Customs

‍

Key Points to Keep in Mind

  • The application must be filed before customs initiates disposal proceedings
  • All accrued storage and handling charges must be settled in full
  • Regulated goods still require the appropriate permits even during the lifting process
  • There is no guarantee of approval - each case is evaluated on its merits

‍

If your shipment is at risk of abandonment, act quickly. The longer you wait, the higher the accrued charges and the lower the chance of recovery. A licensed customs broker can help you navigate the lifting process and deal directly with the Bureau of Customs on your behalf.

Name: Penalties and Seizures in Philippine Customs
Summary: Penalties, surcharges, and seizure procedures imposed by the Bureau of Customs for importation violations in the Philippines.
Post body:
The Customs Modernization and Tariff Act (CMTA) gives the Bureau of Customs the authority to impose penalties, surcharges, and initiate seizure proceedings against importers who fail to comply with customs laws and regulations.

‍

Common Causes of Penalties

  • Misdeclaration of goods (incorrect description, quantity, or value)
  • Undervaluation - declaring a lower customs value than the actual transaction price
  • Misclassification - using the wrong HS Code to reduce duty rates
  • Lack of required permits from regulatory agencies
  • Technical smuggling - importing goods in a way that evades proper customs processing

‍

Types of Penalties

‍

Administrative Fines

Monetary penalties imposed for violations such as misdeclaration, late filing, or incomplete documentation. The amount varies depending on the nature and gravity of the violation.

‍

Surcharges

Additional charges applied on top of unpaid or underpaid duties and taxes, often computed as a percentage of the deficiency.

‍

Seizure and Forfeiture

Goods may be seized by customs if found to be misdeclared, prohibited, or imported without proper permits. Seized goods may be forfeited in favor of the government if violations are proven.

‍

Blacklisting

Importers found to have committed serious violations may be blacklisted, preventing them from transacting with the Bureau of Customs.

‍

Seizure Process

  1. Customs issues a Warrant of Seizure and Detention (WSD) upon finding probable cause of a violation
  2. The importer is notified and given the opportunity to respond
  3. A hearing is conducted before the Collector of Customs
  4. A decision is rendered - goods may be released upon payment of fines, or forfeited if violations are upheld
  5. The importer may appeal the decision to higher customs authorities or the Court of Tax Appeals

‍

Most customs violations are avoidable. Accurate declarations, correct classification, and securing the right permits before your shipment arrives are the basics. A licensed customs broker keeps you on the right side of these requirements.

Name: Understanding Tariff Classification in the Philippines
Summary: How tariff classification works in the Philippines - HS codes, duty rates, common issues, and compliance risks importers should know.
Post body:
Tariff classification is a fundamental part of importation, as it determines the applicable duties, taxes, and regulatory requirements for imported goods. In the Philippines, classification is based on the Harmonized System (HS), an internationally recognized system of product categorization.

‍

What Is Tariff Classification?

Each product is assigned an HS Code, which corresponds to a specific description and duty rate. Accurate classification is essential, as misclassification can result in incorrect duty assessment, penalties, or delays in customs clearance.

‍

Why It Matters

Getting the classification right affects:

  • Duties and taxes payable
  • Compliance with regulations
  • Risk of penalties and audit findings

Even minor errors can lead to reassessment or delays that disrupt your supply chain.

‍

Common Classification Issues

Importers often run into problems like:

  • Using overly broad classifications
  • Misclassifying similar products
  • Relying on supplier descriptions without independent verification

‍

How to Get It Right

Classification should always be based on material composition, function or use, and technical specifications - not just the product name.

‍

Name: Understanding Duties, Taxes, and Fees in Importation
Summary: The difference between duties, taxes, and fees in Philippine importation and how they affect your total landed cost and compliance.
Post body:
In the Philippine importation process, costs are divided into duties, taxes, and fees. Understanding each component is essential for accurate landed cost computation and compliance with the Customs Modernization and Tariff Act.

‍

Duties

Duties are tariffs imposed on imported goods based on their classification under the ASEAN Harmonized Tariff Nomenclature (AHTN). These are calculated as a percentage of the customs value. See Customs Valuation Methods in the Philippines for how that value is determined. Duties are collected by the Bureau of Customs and serve to protect domestic industries and generate government revenue.

‍

Taxes

Taxes refer to internal revenue charges applied to imported goods. The most common is the Value-Added Tax (VAT), currently set at 12%, computed on the total landed cost including duties. Certain goods are also subject to excise taxes. While tax policies are administered by the Bureau of Internal Revenue, collection is carried out by customs at the point of importation.

‍

Fees

Fees are service-related charges incurred during cargo handling and processing. These include:

  • Arrastre charges
  • Wharfage dues
  • Customs processing fees
  • Storage or demurrage charges

These are typically encountered during the release and delivery stage.

‍

Step-by-Step Cost Computation

‍

Step 1: Determine Customs Value (CIF Basis)

CIF = FOB (cost of goods) + Freight + Insurance. This is the foundation of all duty and tax computations.

‍

Step 2: Compute Import Duty

Import Duty = CIF x Duty Rate. Duty rates vary (0%-65%) depending on product classification. Preferential rates may apply with a Certificate of Origin.

‍

Step 3: Compute Other Charges

These may include excise tax (for alcohol, fuel, tobacco, vehicles) and customs processing fees.

‍

Step 4: Compute VAT

VAT = (CIF + Duty + Other Charges) x 12%

‍

Step 5: Add Service Fees

Include arrastre, wharfage, storage, and brokerage fees to arrive at the full landed cost.

‍

Getting the landed cost computation right from the start - see our Importation Costs Breakdown Philippines for a worked example - helps businesses price accurately, plan cash flow, and avoid surprises at the port.

Name: Trailer Chassis Conditioned Tax and Duty Exemption Under CMTA Section 800(Z)
Summary: Learn the rules, conditions, import process, and documentary requirements for the conditional tax and duty exemption of trailer chassis imported by shipping companies under CMTA Section 800(Z) and CAO 06-2020.
Post body:
Trailer chassis imported by shipping companies may qualify for conditional tax and duty exemption under Section 800(Z) of the CMTA. These chassis are used to transport containerized cargo within ports, warehouses, and customs areas, helping improve cargo movement and reduce delays in trade operations. The exemption allows shipping companies to temporarily import trailer chassis without immediate payment of duties and taxes, provided they comply with the conditions set by the Bureau of Customs.

‍

Conditions for the Exemption

Under CMTA Section 800(Z) and CAO 06-2020 Section 5.30, the following conditions must be complied with:

  1. The trailer chassis must be imported by shipping companies only.
  2. The trailer chassis must be used exclusively for handling containerized cargo.
  3. The shipping company must post a security equivalent to 100% of the duties, taxes, and other charges.
  4. The security covers a period of one year from the date of acceptance of the customs entry.
  5. The Commissioner of Customs may extend the period from year to year for valid or meritorious reasons.
  6. The trailer chassis must be properly identified and registered with the Land Transportation Office (LTO).
  7. The importer must pay the customs supervision fee fixed by the District Collector and approved by the Commissioner.
  8. The trailer chassis must remain deposited within the customs territory when not in use.
  9. Upon expiration of the allowed period, the importer must either pay the duties and taxes or re-export the trailer chassis.

‍

Common Documents Needed

  • TEI with accompanying documents
  • Goods Declaration
  • Import Bill of Lading/Air Waybill
  • Import Invoice and Packing List
  • Proof that the importer is a shipping company
  • Certificate or proof of intended exclusive use for containerized cargo
  • Surety Bond or Security Bond equivalent to 100% duties and taxes
  • LTO registration documents
  • Authority or clearance from the Bureau of Customs

‍

Step-by-Step Import Process

  1. Prepare Import Documents - The shipping company gathers the invoice, bill of lading, packing list, and other cargo documents before shipment arrival.
  2. File Import Entry with the BOC - The importer files the customs declaration and applies for conditional tax and duty exemption under CMTA Section 800(Z).
  3. Post the Required Security Bond - The shipping company posts a bond equal to 100% of the estimated duties and taxes.
  4. Register the Trailer Chassis with the LTO - The importer secures proper identification and registration of the chassis.
  5. Customs Inspection and Approval - The Bureau of Customs checks the documents and may inspect the trailer chassis before release.
  6. Use the Trailer Chassis for Containerized Cargo Only - The chassis must only be used for its declared purpose during the approved period.
  7. Monitor the One-Year Validity Period - Before the period expires, the importer may request extension if there are valid reasons.
  8. Re-export or Pay Duties and Taxes Upon Expiration - At the end of the approved period, the shipping company must either re-export the chassis or settle the applicable duties and taxes. Working with a licensed customs broker helps ensure all compliance steps are properly handled.

Name: How to Get Duty Exemptions on Recovered Goods and Salvaged Vessels
Summary: Learn how to import salvaged goods and vessel parts without paying duties. Understand the two-year rule and required documents under the CMTA.
Post body:
When a ship meets with an accident or is left behind in the water, items recovered from it can enter the Philippines without the usual import duties. This rule covers goods found inside, the parts of the foreign ship itself, and even its equipment - whether the vessel was wrecked in Philippine waters or elsewhere. Allowing them to enter duty-free helps maritime companies and salvors recover value from what would otherwise be lost at sea.

‍

Conditions for the Exemption

  • The goods and salvage must come from foreign vessels that were wrecked or abandoned.
  • The wreck or abandonment can happen in Philippine waters or anywhere else in the world.
  • The recovery must happen after a period of at least two (2) years.
  • The two-year clock starts either from the date the marine protest was filed or from the time the vessel was wrecked or abandoned.
  • Any goods or salvage recovered within the two-year period remain dutiable - the importer must pay the full taxes.

‍

Required Documents

  • A Tax and Duty Exemption Indorsement (TEI) with all supporting papers
  • The official Inventory Report made by the Customs Examiner
  • A Certification or Report from MARINA
  • The standard Goods Declaration

‍

Step-by-Step Import Process

‍

1. Monitor the Timeline

The importer tracks the date the ship was wrecked or the date the marine protest was filed. They must wait for the full two-year period to end before claiming the tax exemption. Goods brought in early will be subject to full duty.

‍

2. Conduct the Recovery and Salvage

The importer or salvage team retrieves the goods, parts, or equipment from the foreign vessel and keeps them together for official inspection.

‍

3. Request a MARINA Report

The importer contacts the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) and secures an official certification or report confirming the vessel was wrecked or abandoned.

‍

4. Undergo Customs Inspection

Once the goods are in the custody of the Bureau of Customs, a Customs Examiner performs a physical check and creates an Inventory Report listing exactly what was recovered and its condition.

‍

5. Apply for Tax Exemption (TEI)

The importer files an application for a Tax and Duty Exemption Indorsement (TEI), submitting the MARINA report and the Customs Inventory Report as proof that the shipment meets the legal requirements. A licensed customs broker can help prepare and file the necessary documentation accurately.

‍

6. File the Goods Declaration

The importer submits the Goods Declaration along with the approved TEI, confirming that the items are entering the country legally but exempt from import duties.

‍

7. Release of Goods

After the Bureau of Customs verifies the two-year rule and the documents, they process the clearance and the importer receives the goods.

Name: Aircraft, Parts, Supplies, Etc. of Scheduled Airlines With Congressional Franchise
Summary: Learn the customs duty and tax exemptions for aircraft, parts, supplies, and equipment imported by scheduled airlines with a congressional franchise in the Philippines.
Post body:
Scheduled airlines operating under a congressional franchise in the Philippines may enjoy certain customs tax and duty privileges on the importation of aircraft, parts, supplies, and related equipment. These exemptions are intended to support the aviation industry, improve air transport services, and help airlines maintain efficient and safe operations.

‍

Goods Covered by the Exemption

Eligible airlines with a valid congressional franchise may receive tax and/or duty privileges on the importation of goods directly related to airline operations, such as:

  • Aircraft and airplanes
  • Aircraft engines
  • Spare parts and replacement components
  • Navigation and communication equipment
  • Ground support equipment
  • Aviation tools and maintenance materials
  • Cabin safety equipment
  • Supplies necessary for flight operations

These imported items are generally intended for the use, repair, maintenance, or operation of airline services. For example, if a scheduled airline with a congressional franchise needs imported aircraft spare parts not reasonably available in the Philippines, those parts may be brought in duty-free if necessary for operations.

‍

Conditions for Availment

To qualify for customs privileges, airlines are generally required to comply with applicable laws and regulations, including:

  • Valid congressional franchise
  • Authority to operate from the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines or relevant aviation regulator
  • Proof that imported goods are for airline use
  • Submission of customs import documents to the Bureau of Customs

‍

Common Documents Required

  • TEI with accompanying documents
  • Goods Declaration
  • Bill of Lading or Air Waybill
  • Import Invoice / Packing List

‍

Step-by-Step Import Process

  1. Prepare Supporting Documents - The airline or customs broker gathers all import papers, invoices, permits, and proof that the shipment qualifies for duty exemption.
  2. File Import Documents with the BOC - The importer files the Goods Declaration and supporting documents with the proper customs office.
  3. Submit Proof of Eligibility - The importer presents proof that the airline operates under a congressional franchise and that the imported goods are necessary for airline operations.
  4. Customs Evaluation and Verification - The Bureau of Customs reviews the shipment and supporting papers for compliance with Section 800(V) of the CMTA and CAO 06-2020.
  5. Release of Imported Goods - Once approved, customs releases the imported aircraft parts, supplies, or equipment for use in airline operations.

Name: Food and Beverage Importation in the Philippines
Summary: Complete guide to importing food and beverages into the Philippines, including FDA requirements, permits, and customs clearance process.
Post body:
Importation of food and beverage products into the Philippines is highly regulated to protect public health and ensure product safety. Businesses must comply with requirements from multiple government agencies, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the Bureau of Customs (BOC), and other regulatory bodies depending on the type of product. In many cases, businesses must also secure import permits from the Philippines for regulated goods, particularly those subject to sanitary and phytosanitary controls, before shipment is initiated.

‍

From a customs standpoint, importers must follow the formal customs clearance process, which includes lodging the Goods Declaration, ensuring accurate tariff classification, and paying the appropriate duties and taxes. Proper import documentation is essential at every stage, as incomplete or incorrect paperwork can lead to shipment delays or additional inspections. Documents such as invoices, packing lists, certificates of origin, and permits must be complete and consistent to avoid issues during customs processing.

‍

Common compliance challenges include improper labeling, missing product registration, and failure to secure necessary permits prior to importation. These issues can result in delays, penalties, or even rejection of goods at the border. Because food importation involves both regulatory compliance and customs procedures, businesses must adopt a well-coordinated approach to manage risks effectively. They need:

At arrival:

Customs Clearance Process

Once a shipment arrives in the Philippines, it does not go directly to the warehouse. Instead, it undergoes customs clearance handled by the Bureau of Customs to ensure proper declaration and compliance with regulations.

1. Before the arrival.

Clearance starts before the shipment even lands:

2. Arrival of Shipment

If there are errors here, they tend to surface later so this step needs to be done carefully.

4. Selectivity Lane

  • Yellow Lane - documents are reviewed

If the image is found to be suspicious it will be subject to physical inspection.

  • Red Lane - documents are reviewed, xray scan, and shipment is physically inspected

e. Release of Goods

‍

After Clearance:

‍

  • BOC issues Release Order
  • Goods are released from port/warehouse
  • Transported to your warehouse

f. Post- Clearance Monitoring

‍

Authorities may still:

  • Audit documents

Used to:

How-to-import-goods-philippines

‍

Importing cosmetics and personal care products into the Philippines for commercial purposes is strictly regulated to ensure consumer safety and product quality. The process is overseen by the Food and Drug Administration and the Bureau of Customs. Importers must comply with legal registration, licensing, and product notification requirements before goods can be distributed in the market.

‍

Step-by-Step Guide to Importing Cosmetics

‍

1. Establish a Legal Business Entity

‍

Before importing, you must first register a business in the Philippines. If you are a sole proprietor, registration must be completed with the Department of Trade and Industry. For corporations or partnerships, registration is required with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

‍

Additionally, you must secure a Mayor’s Business Permit and register with the Bureau of Internal Revenue for tax compliance.

‍

2. Secure an FDA License to Operate (LTO)

‍

Importers must obtain a License to Operate (LTO) from the FDA through the Center for Cosmetics Regulation and Research (CCRR). This license authorizes the business to import and distribute cosmetic products.

‍

Key requirements include a notarized application form, Joint Affidavit of Undertaking, proof of a qualified professional (such as a pharmacist), and a warehouse or office inspection. Applications are submitted via the FDA eServices Portal. The initial LTO is valid for one year, while renewals are typically valid for two years.

‍

3. Cosmetic Product Notification (CPN)

‍

Before any cosmetic product can be sold, it must be notified with the FDA. The importer, acting as the Local Company Responsible (LCR), must submit product details through the FDA e-Portal.

‍

Required information includes the product name, complete ingredient list compliant with the ASEAN Cosmetic Directive, manufacturer details, and labeling designs. Once approved, a Cosmetic Product Notification (CPN) certificate is issued, usually valid for one to three years.

‍

4. Prepare Import Documents

‍

Each shipment must be supported by complete documentation for customs processing. These include:

‍

Commercial Invoice or Proforma Invoice

‍

Packing List

‍

Bill of Lading or Airway Bill

‍

Valid FDA LTO and corresponding CPN certificates

‍

Certificate of Analysis (COA) or Certificate of Free Sale

‍

These documents ensure that the imported products meet regulatory and safety standards.

‍

5. Customs Clearance and Product Release

‍

Upon arrival, shipments are processed by the Bureau of Customs. Commercial goods with a value of PHP 50,000 or more are subject to formal entry procedures. Importers must pay applicable duties, value-added tax (VAT), and other processing fees.

‍

The Bureau of Customs also coordinates with the FDA to verify that the products are properly notified before releasing them into the Philippine market.

‍

Key Rules: Personal vs. Commercial Import

‍

Commercial Importation: Requires full compliance, including an LTO and CPN. Products must also be properly labeled with the importer’s name and address.

‍

Personal Use Importation: Cosmetics imported in small quantities for personal use (e.g., limited number of perfumes, lotions, or lipsticks) may be allowed without FDA clearance, especially if brought in as personal baggage or through balikbayan boxes.

‍

Customs-clearance-process-philippines

‍

The customs clearance process for cosmetics and personal care products in the Philippines is a mandatory multi-phase procedure handled primarily by the Bureau of Customs and the Food and Drug Administration. For commercial shipments, importers must follow these stages to avoid delays, penalties, or seizure of goods.

‍

1. Pre-Lodgment (Regulatory Compliance)

‍

Before shipment arrival, all regulatory requirements must be secured. Importers must obtain a License to Operate (LTO) from the FDA as an importer or distributor. In addition, each product must have a Cosmetic Product Notification (CPN) filed through the FDA e-portal. Importers are also required to register with the Bureau of Customs through the Client Profile Registration System (CPRS).

‍

2. Declaration (Electronic Lodgment)

‍

Once the shipment arrives, a Goods Declaration must be filed through the Electronic-to-Mobile (e2m) Customs System, usually by a licensed customs broker using a Value Added Service Provider (VASP).

‍

There are two types of entries:

‍

  • Formal Entry - for shipments with an FOB/FCA value of PHP 50,000 or more
  • Informal Entry - for shipments valued below PHP 50,000

‍

Required documents include the Bill of Lading (B/L) or Airway Bill (AWB), commercial invoice, packing list, and valid FDA LTO and CPN certificates.

‍

3. Assessment and Selectivity

‍

The Bureau of Customs evaluates shipments using a Selectivity System to determine the level of inspection:

‍

  • Green Lane - no inspection (automatic release)
  • Yellow Lane - documentary review
  • Red Lane - physical and documentary inspection

‍

Customs also verifies the correct classification under the ASEAN Harmonized Tariff Nomenclature (AHTN) or HS Code to determine applicable duties and taxes.

‍

4. Payment of Duties and Taxes

‍

After assessment, importers must settle duties and taxes through Authorized Agent Banks (AAB). Customs duties typically range from 3% to 30%, depending on the product classification. A 12% Value-Added Tax (VAT) is applied to the total landed cost.

‍

Shipments valued at PHP 10,000 or below may qualify for the de minimis rule, making them exempt from duties and taxes.

‍

5. Final Release

‍

Once payment is confirmed, the On-Line Release System (OLRS) authorizes the release of the shipment. The cargo is then turned over to the importer or their authorized representative by the port or warehouse operator.

‍

Summary of BOC Charges

‍

Charge Type

‍

  • Customs Duty
  • Depend on HS Code
  • Vat
  • 12% of Landed Cost
  • Import Processing
  • Php 250 to Php 1000 (based on value)
  • Customs Documentary Stamp
  • Php 265 (fixed rate)

‍

Import-duties-taxes-philippines

‍

Importing cosmetics and personal care products into the Philippines involves applicable duties and taxes regulated by the Bureau of Customs. These charges are primarily composed of customs duties and Value-Added Tax (VAT), which are computed based on the total landed cost of the goods.

‍

In general, imported cosmetics are subject to a 12% Value-Added Tax (VAT) and an average duty rate of around 5.7%, although the exact duty depends on the product’s tariff classification. Some products may be subject to higher rates (up to 65%) or reduced to zero if covered by a valid Certificate of Origin under applicable trade agreements.

‍

A key rule to consider is the de minimis threshold. Shipments with a Free on Board (FOB) or Free Carrier (FCA) value of ₱10,000 or below are exempt from both duties and VAT. This makes small-value imports more cost-efficient, especially for personal purchases.

‍

For personal use importation, cosmetics such as lotions, soaps, and similar items may be exempt from clearance by the Food and Drug Administration, provided they are in limited quantities (typically not exceeding 1 kilogram per product). Exceeding this threshold may classify the goods as commercial, requiring full regulatory compliance and potentially leading to seizure if requirements are not met.

‍

Another important provision applies to balikbayan boxes. Qualified overseas Filipinos may avail of duty- and tax-free privileges for personal effects sent up to three times per year, with a maximum declared value of ₱150,000 per shipment, subject to existing regulations.

‍

Typical Cost Summary

‍

  • Import Duty: Varies depending on HS code (commonly around 5.7%, but may reach up to 65%)
  • VAT: 12% of the total landed cost
  • Fees: Includes fixed Bureau of Customs charges such as:
  • ₱40.00 Import Entry and Internal Revenue Declaration (IEIRD) fee
  • ₱265.00 Customs Documentary Stamp (CDS)

Goods for making or recording motion picture films include equipment, devices, tools, and materials directly used to create, shoot, record, edit, or produce film and audiovisual content. Production companies, film outfits, media entities, and international film crews often import these goods temporarily for specific projects in the Philippines. The BOC may grant a conditional exemption from duties and taxes when importers bring these goods into the country for film production purposes and comply with customs requirements.

Requirements

  2. Affidavit by foreign film producers stating that the goods are not for sale, barter, or hire but are directly and exclusively used for making or recording motion pictures on location in the Philippines, with an itemized list of goods and their values
  3. Identification, examination and appraisal by a customs officer and the issuance of a Certificate of Identification
  4. Security equal to 100% of the ascertained duties, taxes and other charges, conditioned for exportation or payment within three (3) months from the date of acceptance of the goods declaration, unless extended by the District Collector for another three (3) months
  5. Goods Declaration
  6. Import Bill of Lading/Air Waybill
  7. Import Invoice/Packing List

‍

How to Qualify for Conditional Duty Exemption

‍

1. Identify the Goods and Confirm Eligibility

Before shipment, review the imported goods and confirm that they directly support film production. Prepare a complete inventory of equipment and technical specifications, including serial numbers, descriptions, and intended production use. Early preparation reduces customs delays.

‍

2. Prepare Documentary Requirements

Gather all importation and production-related documents before the shipment arrives. Make sure the information remains accurate and consistent across all records. Mismatched declarations often delay customs processing.

‍

3. File the Application for Conditional Exemption

Submit the required application and supporting documents to the appropriate customs office. Clearly explain the nature of the film project, the purpose of the imported goods, the duration of use in the Philippines, and the planned re-export schedule. Engaging a licensed customs broker familiar with temporary importations can streamline this step.

‍

4. Post the Required Bond or Security

Once customs officers assess the shipment, comply with any bond or security requirement. The BOC uses this safeguard to ensure compliance with customs obligations. Failure to post the required bond may delay cargo release.

‍

5. Secure Customs Approval and Release

After reviewing the documents and confirming compliance, customs authorities may approve the conditional exemption and release the goods. Keep copies of all approvals and customs records throughout the production period.

‍

6. Re-export the Goods or Complete Final Customs Compliance

After filming ends, re-export the equipment within the prescribed period or comply with any approved customs disposition process. Submit proof of compliance to facilitate bond cancellation or release. Missing deadlines may result in duties, taxes, and penalties.
